records.mutation: audit each case-deletion for a fact the constrained party lacks, and require applying every constraint to both members of the pair so the balanced/symmetric case gets tested
records.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling with the incumbent scored 1/8; 4 of 8 truncated and all eight burned 14k-16.4k tokens. Seven failures immediately deleted the additive branch by claiming a party who knows one aggregate and their own value can always deduce the partner, then enumerated only factor pairs of the given number, refuted all of them, and reported a refuted factor or one they admitted was recalled from a classic puzzle. The lone success was the one rollout that stayed in the additive branch and reached the balanced split. So instead of the incumbent's intersect-across-readings clause I added a deletion audit (a case dies only if the constrained party really has that fact) plus a rule to impose every constraint on both members of the pair, which is what points at the symmetric candidate no factor enumeration reaches.

records.mutation: promote undetermined coefficients (posit the general form of the requested object, pin coefficients from cheap exact instances) as the primary technique, replacing further tuning of the recheck loop
records.subagent_summary: Seven of eight rollouts were correct in 5.8k-9.1k tokens; the failure had the correct locus and radius by ~3k tokens, then spot-checked a root by inverting a purely imaginary number while keeping its modulus instead of inverting it, so a sound derivation appeared to contradict itself and it burned the remaining 13k tokens re-auditing without ever recording a result. Rounds 5-10 all attacked that audit loop with meta-discipline (bound the checking, name the arithmetic rule, reorder commit before verify) and every one lost transfer, while the only proposal that ever beat the incumbent on transfer carried a concrete constructive technique. So I stop tuning the loop and add reusable machinery: when the requested object has a known form, posit that form with unknown coefficients and pin them from a few cheap exact instances rather than pushing a parametrization through trig, keeping the setup and a compressed no-restart clause.

records.mutation: front-load the combining arithmetic into the first visible step instead of a generic transcribe-don't-rederive rule, and generalize the obvious-step caution to small-case testing
records.subagent_summary: Two of eight scored, a drop from the incumbent's five, but no failure was mathematical: seven of eight reached the correct value inside the first 3-7k of ~55-62k characters. Four never closed reasoning at all while still numerically re-testing rotations (98-182 rotation mentions, 45-83 restarts). The two decisive cases both closed reasoning and began a tidy headed write-up, but spent their whole visible budget re-establishing coordinates and re-arguing which configuration is minimal, and were truncated mid-sentence one step short of combining the numbers; both successes reached that same combining step. So the incumbent's transcribe-not-rederive clause fires too late to matter. This revision orders the write-up explicitly: do the sum-minus-overlap arithmetic in the very first visible step, and broadens the obvious-step warning to small-case testing for transfer.

records.mutation: pin the shared affine target to position rather than piece label; contrast the d root cap with the d+1 interpolation count; replace the open-ended count audit with a no-re-litigation directive
records.subagent_summary: 5 of 8 fresh rollouts were correct and all three failures were pure token-limit truncations rather than wrong counts, so the residual-root and reusability framing is landing and the remaining loss is budget discipline. One truncated rollout indexed the affine target by which piece was used instead of by position in the pattern, then spiralled trying to force the piece labels themselves into a progression; the other two oscillated between the degree-d root cap and the d+1 points that determine a polynomial, re-deriving both without committing. The revision therefore pins the index to position and bans piece-label indexing, states the d-versus-d+1 distinction in one clause, and replaces the incumbent's open-ended 'check your count uses every number given' audit - which invites reopening an already-proved bound - with an up-front instruction not to re-litigate settled steps.

records.mutation: delete the misfiring out-of-domain clause; replace it with a jam-free rule that a root reproducing given data is a setup artifact, so take the other
records.subagent_summary: 7 of 8 fresh rollouts were correct and all eight terminated normally under 12k tokens, so budget death is no longer the failure mode. The single failure reduced correctly to the right two-root equation, then declared one root out of the domain by appealing to an interval it recalled wrongly, kept the root that merely reproduced a point it had already been given, watched the figure collapse, and reported that collapse as the value. This is the third round with that exact signature. Rounds 6 and 10 both tried to repair the domain clause by demanding substitution over recall, and both lost transfer, so this time I delete that clause instead of patching it: a root that only reproduces given data is an artifact of your own setup, so use the other. Length stays near the incumbent, since brevity is the only edit that has ever gained here.

records.mutation: encode histories as words over move types with legality as a prefix inequality; free 50/50 steps only where both letters stay legal, and slot questions resolved by a derived arrival index plus shortest forcing prefix
records.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling with the incumbent gave 1/8; seven rollouts stopped normally at 12k-15k tokens and one hit the cap, so length is secondary. Six of eight reached a 2^(free) atom count on the first part then abandoned it on the second: each of those equated the destination pile bottom slot with the item delivered last and asserted every item was equally likely there, reading off 1/4 or 1/2. Two also mis-sized the atom set itself (16 branches, or 4! permutations) because they never tested which steps were legal. The only correct rollout kept one atom set for both parts. The revision replaces the vague first-versus-last hedge with a concrete encoding: a history is a word over move types, legality is a prefix inequality, a step is free only where both letters stay legal, and slot questions are resolved by deriving the arrival index from the stated placement rule and pricing the shortest forcing prefix.

records.mutation: add honest sizing rule for the reduced instance (as many conditions as unknowns, inconsistency means an off-by-one exponent range, never conclude unsolvable) and reframe a leftover free constant as an unused given
records.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling under the incumbent scored 0 of 8 with 7 of 8 hitting the token cap. Every rollout recast the setup as a long product times a linear factor, then stalled trying to pin two constants from one condition; several concluded the data was insufficient or that the problem was broken, and the one that terminated forced a constant to zero and landed on a wrong value. Two attempted the small-case route that has produced every past success, but built the miniature with one more exponent condition than unknowns, got a contradictory tiny system, and abandoned the route rather than fixing the range. The revision keeps commit-then-verify but adds an explicit sizing rule for the reduced instance, routes inconsistency to an off-by-one repair, blocks the unsolvable exit, and reframes an unpinnable constant as a signal that a given is still unused.

records.mutation: keep the incumbent verbatim and append an output-form discipline clause (answer the quantity asked, exact reduced form, one simplified number, no decimal or intermediate)
records.subagent_summary: Round 11 sampling again returned 8/8 correct with clean stops at 3.0-6.7k tokens, so train has been pinned at 1.0 for eleven straight rounds and only transfer can move J. The rollouts still solve this question correctly but burn most of their length arguing about which value the setup intends, then close cleanly; the closing sentence is the only clause doing transferable work. Prior rounds already tested anti-rumination, gcd naming, scope labeling and representation-switching tails and all lost held-out ground, so this round leaves the incumbent untouched and appends the one unexplored axis: output-form discipline. Many failures on unfamiliar problems are correct reasoning reported in the wrong form (unreduced fraction, decimalized radical, an expression, or an intermediate quantity), which a grader marks wrong regardless of the work.

records.mutation: order recentering before any exploration, forbid re-expansion into standard powers when evaluating requested inputs, and treat a degenerate center or failed numeric check as a one-line arithmetic slip rather than refutation
records.subagent_summary: Only 3 of 8 fresh rollouts were correct: four ran to the token cap and one terminated wrong. Every failure reached the shared-center antisymmetric form yet left it. Two spent 10k+ tokens surveying inverses and general coefficients before recentering, then hit the cap just as the centered solve worked. Two mis-added the given values, got a degenerate center, read that as refutation, and reverted to expanding the degree-nine composition. The wrong one solved the center correctly, then rewrote the centered form into standard powers and re-added the given constant the center already encodes, so a correct value became wrong. The revision therefore orders recentering first, forbids evaluating outside the centered form, and reclassifies any degenerate center or failed spot-check as one slipped line to recheck rather than grounds to abandon the structure.

records.mutation: require the smallest nontrivial count be confirmed two independent ways (iterate the whole row vs. follow one label home) before any pattern is fit, and forbid a moved block from silently reverting to its starting internal order
records.subagent_summary: 3 of 8 scored, but the split is not about strategy: every rollout that reasoned at all built a corrupted table of small-case counts and never rechecked it. Four hit the token cap; one finished on an exponent one too small purely because its second-smallest count was wrong; one wrote a row that was not even a rearrangement of the row above (a block reverted to its starting internal order), called it 'very confusing', and looped; another produced a map sending four inputs to one image. The three successes matched no table they had computed, so they were guesses. The incumbent already forbids piecewise splits and untraced period claims, which is why the student never doubts its earliest bad count. The revision therefore forces the smallest nontrivial count to be confirmed two independent ways before generalizing, and names the block-reverts-to-original-order slip that produces the impossible rows.
